options: An ordinary DataFrame, which supports every DataFrame method used throughout this chapter
A plain Python string containing the query results
A special SQL-only object with no DataFrame methods available
Nothing — it only prints results directly to the console
questions.explain: You can chain .select(), .filter(), .show(), etc. on the result exactly as if you'd built it with the DataFrame API.

questions.q: Why does the same query written as SQL vs. as chained DataFrame methods perform identically?
options: Both compile down to the exact same Catalyst execution plan, per Lesson 38
The DataFrame API is always faster because it skips SQL parsing
They don't perform identically; SQL is significantly slower in practice
SQL is always faster because it's compiled ahead of time
questions.explain: This is straight back to Lesson 38's core point about the two APIs sharing an execution engine underneath.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when does a query tend to read more naturally as SQL?
options: SQL syntax is never more readable than DataFrame methods in any case
A query with several joins and a WHERE clause, especially for someone with a SQL background
Only when no aggregation is involved at all
Only when the data has fewer than 100 rows
questions.explain: A query built up step by step often reads more clearly as chained DataFrame methods instead — there's no fixed rule.

questions.q: Can a real pipeline mix the DataFrame API and Spark SQL within the same script?
options: Yes — clean with the DataFrame API, register as a temp view, then query with SQL (or the reverse), freely switching back and forth
Mixing them causes a runtime error
Only if the DataFrame was originally read from a SQL database
No, a script must commit to exactly one API for its entire lifetime
questions.explain: Nothing stops you from switching between the two approaches within the same pipeline.

questions.q: What must happen before you can query a DataFrame with spark.sql()?
options: Nothing — spark.sql() works on any DataFrame automatically
It must be written to disk as a Parquet file first
It must first be converted to a Pandas DataFrame
It must be registered with createOrReplaceTempView(), per Lesson 58
questions.explain: This directly reuses Lesson 58's setup step — without a registered view, there's nothing for the SQL query to reference.
